A1-A2.headline: The Ancient Path of Northern Gold

pages.text: Long ago, people traveled on a special path. This was the Amber Road. It went from the cold Baltic Sea to the warm Mediterranean Sea. Traders moved amber, a beautiful stone, along this way. People called it the gold of the north.
pages.caption: The ancient route from the Baltic to the Mediterranean.

evidence.articleCaption: The ancient route from the Baltic Sea to the areas of the Roman Empire by the Mediterranean Sea

pages.text: This trade started a long time ago. We know this because of old items found in Egypt and Greece. Kings and queens loved amber. They used it for jewelry. It was a very important item for many different people in ancient times.

The Roman Empire used this road too. It was good for trade and for the army. Romans built walls to keep the traders safe from raids. The road went through many lands. It helped connect the north to the south for many years.

Today, we find much amber in the ground. In one place, experts found over 1,000 kilograms of it. This is a very big find. We still study this old road to learn about how people lived and worked together long ago.
pages.caption: Amber deposits found in different parts of Europe.

B1-B2.headline: Tracing the Ancient Amber Road Across Europe

pages.text: Imagine a path stretching from the cold Baltic shores to the warm Mediterranean. This was the famous trade route for fossilized resin, often called the gold of the north. For thousands of years, this network linked distant cultures and helped goods flow between northern and southern Europe.
pages.caption: The ancient route from the Baltic to the Mediterranean.

evidence.articleCaption: The ancient route from the Baltic Sea to the areas of the Roman Empire by the Mediterranean Sea

pages.text: Historical records show that trade began by the 16th century BC. Experts have found Baltic resin in sites as far away as Egypt and Mycenae. This proves the material was highly valued by ancient people for its beauty and its status as a rare luxury item in the Mediterranean region.

During the Roman era, the route became vital for both business and military movement. The Romans built defensive walls along the path to keep merchants safe from local attacks. The road connected diverse regions, including modern-day Poland and Italy, allowing for the exchange of goods like glass and metals.

Modern research continues to reveal the scale of this trade. In Wrocław, experts found a massive deposit of resin, estimated between 1,240 and 1,760 kilograms. This discovery suggests a large volume of trade, though the exact total remains uncertain due to the nature of historical record-keeping.
pages.caption: Amber deposits found in different parts of Europe.

C1-C2.headline: The Amber Road: A Conduit of Ancient Continental Exchange

pages.text: Spanning from the Baltic and North Sea coasts to the Mediterranean, the Amber Road functioned as a critical prehistoric trade corridor. Often dubbed the gold of the north, amber was a cornerstone of early economic interaction, bridging the gap between northern European sources and the sophisticated markets of the Mediterranean basin.
pages.caption: The ancient route from the Baltic to the Mediterranean.

evidence.articleCaption: The ancient route from the Baltic Sea to the areas of the Roman Empire by the Mediterranean Sea

pages.text: The antiquity of this trade is well-documented, with evidence dating back to the 16th century BC. Spectroscopic analysis confirms that Baltic amber reached as far as the Egyptian court of Tutankhamen and the Mycenaean centers. Such findings underscore the extensive reach of these early mercantile networks across the ancient world.

Under Roman administration, the route evolved into a strategic military and commercial artery. Roman authorities erected fortifications to safeguard merchants against regional instability, effectively integrating the Baltic periphery into the imperial economy. While these measures facilitated a robust exchange of northern raw materials for luxury items, the full extent of this trade remains subject to scholarly debate due to the fragmentary nature of the archaeological record.

Archaeological excavations have provided tangible evidence of this historical commerce, most notably the colossal deposit in Wrocław. With estimates ranging from 1,240 to 1,760 kilograms, this find serves as a testament to the sheer scale of the amber trade, illustrating the historical interconnectedness of European regions through this legendary route.
